title: Sky authorizes every distinct emergency power through the same reusable four-part template
content:
A.1.10.5.2.3 (Standby Spells) and A.1.10.5.3.2 (Protego) are near-verbatim duplicates of one another across their entire structure:

1. **Initiation** — reserved for the Core Facilitator, only in response to a properly validated and categorized emergency, ideally after consulting relevant Scope Advisors, with TechOps triggering the Emergency Response Group afterwards (A.1.10.5.2.3.1 / A.1.10.5.3.2.1).
2. **Acknowledgement and attestation** — Core GovOps must acknowledge receipt, and two named Authorized Representatives must validate the artifact's authenticity in writing (A.1.10.5.2.3.2 / A.1.10.5.3.2.2).
3. **Delegate preconditions** — ADs must confirm notification, decision and validation before voting, then vote promptly or state concerns (A.1.10.5.2.3.3 / A.1.10.5.3.2.3).
4. **Penalty and fallback** — identical derecognition-plus-buffer-confiscation clause, and an identical exception for unresponsive Core GovOps.

The repetition is itself the finding. Rather than designing bespoke controls per capability, Sky has one **emergency authorization template** and instantiates it for each power. The powers differ enormously — Standby Spells fire circuit breakers, Protego cancels pending votes — but the human process around them is deliberately uniform.

The benefit is that responders execute one memorized procedure under stress instead of recalling which controls attach to which tool, and reviewers audit one process. The risk is coupled failure: a flaw in the template, such as the single-appointed-validator fallback, appears simultaneously in every power built from it. Uniformity trades independent failure modes for reduced cognitive load in exactly the moment when cognitive load kills.
description: Standby Spells and Protego share an identical process: Core Facilitator initiation on a validated incident, Core GovOps written attestation, AD preconditions, and one fixed breach penalty.
